kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer_part_number: none published by ELEGOO; functionally equivalent to Adafruit Piezo Buzzer PS1240 (PID 160)
generic_equivalents: Handson Technology KY-006-style Passive Buzzer Module core element (SKU MDU1126)

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A tiny speaker with no brain of its own; it only makes sound if you feed it a changing (PWM) signal, which lets it play different notes and even simple songs.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Playing tones and melodies under program control using the Arduino tone() function or a manually generated square wave.
function.how_it_works_briefly: A thin piezo disc bends back and forth in step with the square wave applied to it; the speed of that back-and-forth motion is what you hear as pitch. Feed it 523 Hz and you hear middle C, feed it 1047 Hz and you hear a note an octave higher.

pinout.notes: red wire in ELEGOO's own wiring diagram; connects to UNO digital pin 8
black wire in ELEGOO's own wiring diagram; connects to GND

pins.pin_1_identification: ELEGOO's tutorial states explicitly: red (positive) wire to pin 8, black (negative) wire to GND. On the bare part, the positive lead is the longer of the two pins.

electrical.operating_voltage: 3-5V DC (per the Handson Technology passive buzzer module datasheet, a close equivalent element)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: not published by ELEGOO; the Adafruit PS1240 equivalent element is rated for drive signals up to 30V peak-to-peak
electrical.typical_current: a few mA; a piezo element draws very little current and is typically driven directly from a microcontroller pin
electrical.max_current: not published for this exact part
electrical.logic_level: 5V, driven directly from an UNO digital/PWM pin

key_specs.frequency_range_hz: approximately 1500-2500 Hz typical drive range (per the Handson Technology passive buzzer module datasheet); ELEGOO's own example lesson plays notes from 523 Hz to 1047 Hz
key_specs.note: must not be driven with analogWrite(), whose fixed 500 Hz PWM rate does not match musical notes; use the tone() function instead

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small round can about 12mm in diameter, with two pins sticking out of the bottom.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Shows a visible green circuit board (PCB) on the back/bottom, unlike the active buzzer's solid black sealed back.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: None typically visible; component markings may be printed on the small green PCB.
easily_confused_with: Active buzzer (near-identical size and shape, but has a solid black seal instead of a visible green PCB, and does not need a changing signal to sound)

example_connections.uno_pin: Digital pin 8 (per ELEGOO's Lesson 7 wiring diagram)

required_extra_parts: the pitches.h Arduino library used by the example sketch
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: pitches.h (defines note-frequency constants; used together with the built-in tone() function)

hazards: None significant; a low-voltage, low-current part
handling_notes: Do not drive with analogWrite(); its fixed 500 Hz rate will not produce the intended musical tones
Observe polarity for a reliable connection, though piezo elements are less sensitive to reversal than active buzzers
common_mistakes: Wiring it like an active buzzer (steady digitalWrite HIGH) and getting no sound or just a click
Forgetting to install the pitches.h library before uploading the example sketch

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: No sound when using an active-buzzer style sketch
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Passive buzzers need a changing signal, not steady power
symptoms_and_causes.check: Confirm the sketch calls tone() rather than just digitalWrite(pin, HIGH)
Reinstall the pitches library as described in Lesson 1 of the ELEGOO tutorial

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Sound is distorted or very quiet
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Wrong wiring, or a genuinely faulty piezo element
symptoms_and_causes.check: Verify the red wire is on D8 and the black wire is on GND, then swap in a known-good buzzer to compare

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: A piezo element behaves like a capacitor, not a resistor, so a standard resistance reading is not meaningful. The simplest multimeter check is AC voltage mode across the two pins while a tone() sketch runs; a small fluctuating AC voltage confirms the UNO is actually driving it.

sources.title: Elegoo Super Starter Kit for UNO tutorial PDF (Lesson 7: Passive Buzzer)
sources.used_for: confirms exact UNO wiring (red to pin 8, black to GND), function, the note frequencies used in the example, and the pitches.h library requirement

sources.title: Passive Buzzer Module datasheet, Handson Technology
sources.used_for: generic-equivalent electrical specs: operating_voltage and frequency_range_hz

sources.title: Piezo Buzzer - PS1240, Adafruit product #160
sources.used_for: bare 2-pin generic equivalent confirming drive voltage range, physical size, and unit_price_usd

confidence.notes: Wiring to the UNO (pin 8, GND) and the visual identification (green PCB vs black seal) both come directly from ELEGOO's own tutorial text. Voltage/frequency specs use a similar Handson Technology module datasheet as the closest available generic reference, since no datasheet exists for a bare 2-pin unbranded buzzer, so treat current draw figures as approximate.
